passages.text: Maternal plasma phospholipid polyunsaturated fatty acids in early pregnancy and thyroid function throughout pregnancy: a longitudinal study
Background
Evidence has indicated that polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs)-enriched diet could reduce inflammation because of thyroid autoimmunity in vivo, and therefore, enhance thyroid function.
Objectives
We investigated whether early pregnancy plasma phospholipid PUFAs could benefit maternal thyroid function across pregnancy, which is critical to fetal brain development and growth in pregnancy.
Methods

Within the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Fetal Growth Studies-Singleton Cohort, we collected plasma samples longitudinally from 214 subjects [107 with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) matched with 107 controls] with a singleton pregnancy. We measured 11 PUFAs at early pregnancy (10-14 wk) and 5 thyroid biomarkers at 10-14, 15-26, 23-31, and 33-39 wk, including free thyroxine (fT4), free triiodothyronine (fT3), thyroid-stimulating hormone, antithyroid peroxidase, and antithyroglobulin. Associations of PUFAs with thyroid function biomarkers and relative risk (RR) of gestational hypothyroidism (GHT) during pregnancy were assessed using generalized linear mixed models and modified Poisson regression, respectively.
Results

After sample weighting because of subjects with GDM over-representing in the analytic sample with biomarkers, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) at early pregnancy was associated with a reduction of 0.24 pmol/L (95% confidence intervals: -0.31, -0.16) in fT3 across gestation per standard deviation (SD) increment, whereas docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) at early pregnancy was associated with an increment of 0.04 ng/dL (0.02, 0.05) in fT4 across gestation per SD increment. Furthermore, EPA and docosatetraenoic acid (DTA) were associated with lower risks of persistent GHT (EPA:RR: 0.13; 0.06, 0.28; DTA:RR: 0.24; 0.13, 0.44) per SD increment. All significant associations remained robust in sensitivity analysis and multiple testing.
Conclusions

Certain plasma phospholipid PUFAs were associated with optimal levels of thyroid biomarkers and even lower risk of GHT throughout pregnancy, which might be potentially targeted for maternal thyroid regulation in early pregnancy.
Clinical Trial Registry
This trial was registered at https://beta.clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00912132?distance=50&term=NCT00912132&rank=1 as NCT00912132.
Introduction

Thyroid function plays a vital role in maintaining a healthy pregnancy as it regulates 3 key pathways: glucose metabolism, lipid metabolism, and protein synthesis. Throughout pregnancy, the thyroid gland enlarges by 40% and experiences an upsurge in the production of thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). If this compensation is disrupted during pregnancy because of maternal pre-existing conditions or environmental risks, it can result in impaired thyroid function, which in severe cases may lead to adverse fetal outcomes including pregnancy loss.

Among the 2 major types of dysfunctional thyroid function, gestational hypothyroidism (GHT) is more commonly observed during pregnancy than gestational hyperthyroidism (~2%-3% compared with 0.1%-0.4%). It is commonly defined as a combination of subclinical hypothyroidism and isolated hypothyroxinemia. GHT results in an imbalance in the concentration of circulating thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), T3, and T4, leading to insufficient levels of thyroid hormones. This condition is associated with adverse maternal outcomes such as preeclampsia and gestational diabetes, as well as detrimental effects on offspring, including low birth weight and impaired neuro-cognitive development, which can manifest as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism.

Although the exact pathogenesis of GHT remains unclear, it is hypothesized that the hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis fails to adapt to the increased demands of thyroxine during pregnancy. Other proposed mechanisms include reduced thyroidal capacity, decreased blood supply to the thyroid, pre-existing impaired thyroid function such as iodine deficiency, and the presence of thyroid autoimmune antibodies such as antithyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and antithyroglobulin (anti-TG) prior to conception. Because thyroid hormones are believed to interact with fatty acid (FA) metabolism and mitochondrial oxidation, emerging evidence suggests that increased consumption of PUFAs (for example, the Mediterranean diet) could potentially benefit individuals with hypothyroidism. This could potentially be attributed to the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties derived from dietary PUFAs. Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge the existing limitations within the current body of literature. Particularly noteworthy is the lack of research focusing on pregnant individuals, as well as the reliance on dietary PUFAs rather than circulating PUFAs. The former approach is susceptible to bias stemming from the subjective nature of the data collection process. Furthermore, there remains a scarcity of evidence delineating the distinct effects of n-3 and n-6 PUFAs concerning thyroid function.

Therefore, it is imperative to explore the potential beneficial correlation between plasma phospholipid PUFAs, considering both exogenous and endogenous sources, and maternal thyroid function throughout pregnancy. Our study aimed to address this research gap by investigating the relationship between early pregnancy plasma phospholipid PUFAs and the trajectory of thyroid function as well as GHT throughout pregnancy, in a multiethnic birth cohort in the United States. We hypothesized that anti-inflammatory n-3 PUFAs would exhibit a positive association, yet proinflammatory n-6 PUFAs would show an inverse association with optimal thyroid function in pregnant subjects.
Methods
Study population and design

The study utilized data from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute Child Health and Human Development Fetal Growth Studies-Singletons cohort, conducted between July 2009 and January 2013. This prospective cohort consisted of 2802 pregnant subjects aged 18-40 y, who did not have major pre-existing chronic diseases such as diabetes or cancer. The participants were recruited between 8 and 13 wk of gestation from 12 clinical centers across the United States. A detailed account of the recruitment process and study protocol has been previously published. For our analysis, we included 214 subjects without pre-existing thyroid dysfunction from a nested case-control study within the primary cohort. Among these participants, 107 were diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) according to the Carpenter and Coustan criteria, as recommended by the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecologists. The remaining 107 individuals served as healthy controls and were matched with the GDM group based on maternal age (+-2 y), self-identified race, and ethnic groups (that is, non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Pacific Islander), and gestational age (GA) at blood collection (+-2 wk) (Supplemental Figure 1).

The primary and substudy of this research received approval from the institutional review boards at all participating sites. Prior to data collection, written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Subsequently, the clinical centers involved in the study entered various study documents and data, including ultrasound measurements and images, into the Clinical Trial Management System. These records were then electronically transferred to the Data Coordinating Center.
Plasma phospholipid PUFA assessments

On enrollment at 10-14 wk (visit 0), blood samples were collected from all participants and biospecimens were stored at -80 C until they were thawed immediately before analysis. The extraction of plasma phospholipid FAs followed the previously described chloroform/methanol method. In brief, lipids were extracted using a mixture of chloroform and methanol (in a 2:1 ratio by volume), and subclasses were separated through thin-layer chromatography. The phospholipid fraction was isolated and converted into methyl esters through derivatization. The resulting product was dissolved in heptane and injected onto a single capillary Varian CP7420 100-m column, connected to a Hewlett Packard 5890 gas chromatograph. The gas chromatograph was configured with a flame ionization detector and used Hewlett Packard chemstation software for data analysis. The individual FA content was expressed as a weight percentage (%) of the total plasma phospholipid FA fraction. All the case-control matched samples were assayed within the same analytical assay, albeit in a random order. In addition, we performed 40 repetitions using the pooled control samples from the same cohort in-house to determine the inter-assay coefficients of variation (CVs). The reported inter-assay CVs in our study were consistent with the readings previously reported among pregnant individuals.

We identified 11 plasma phospholipid PUFAs in this study. These included 4 n-3 PUFAs: alpha-linolenic acid (ALA; 18:3n3), EPA (20:5n3), n-3 docosapentaenoic acid (n-3 DPA; 22:5n3) and DHA (22:6n3); and 7 n-6 PUFAs: linoleic acid (LA: 18:2n6), gamma-linolenic acid (GLA; 18:3n6), eicosadienoic acid (EDA; 20:2n6), dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA; 20:3n6), arachidonic acid (AA; 20:4n6), docosatetraenoic acid (DTA; 22:4n6), and n-6 docosapentaenoic acid (n-6 DPA; 22:5n6). The mean and SD for individual weight percentage (%) of PUFAs referencing total FAs were shown in Supplemental Table 1. The inter-assay CVs of individual plasma phospholipid PUFAs as reported in this study were consistently below 11% for all compounds (ALA 10.9%, n-3 DPA 10.4%, DHA 5.4%, LA 2.8%, GLA 10.7%, EDA 5.9%, DGLA 4.5%, AA 4.8%, and n-6 DPA 9.0%). Notably, EPA (22.1%) and DTA (29.9%) exhibited higher CVs, likely attributable to their relatively low abundance during pregnancy.
Assessment of thyroid function biomarkers between 10 and 40 wk of gestation

Blood samples were obtained at 4 distinct time points during pregnancy: gestational weeks 10-14 (visit 0), 15-26 (visit 1), 24-31 (visit 2), and 33-39 (visit 4). Fasting blood samples were collected at visit 1 (15-26 wk of gestation) after an overnight fast of 8-14 h, whereas the remaining samples were obtained randomly during research visits. Plasma concentrations of TSH (mIU/L), free triiodothyronine (fT3) (pmol/L), free thyroxine (fT4) (ng/dL), anti-TG (IU/mL), and anti-TPO (IU/mL) were determined using the electrochemiluminescence immunoassay method using Roche reagents (Roche Diagnostics) on the Roche Cobas e411 analyzer. The plasma ratio of fT3/fT4 ratio was calculated accordingly based on pg/dL over ng/dL (pg/ng). Thyroid markers were measured at all 4 blood collection time points in both GDM cases and nonGDM controls. The assays were conducted in a central laboratory at the University of Minnesota, with the personnel blinded to the case-control status. The inter-assay CVs were <=5% for the thyroid hormones (fT3, fT4, and TSH) and <=15% for the anti-TPO and anti-TG. The plot depicting the median concentration of thyroid function indices overtime during pregnancy has been previously published.

We applied the pregnancy-specific reference range in our study participants for TSH, as per the 2017 American Thyroid Association guidelines. Subjects with TSH concentrations <=4 mIU/L were classified as having normal TSH levels. Subjects with normal TSH status and fT4 concentrations (between the 10th and 90th percentiles in controls) were categorized as euthyroid. GHT is classified as the combination of subclinical hypothyroidism and isolated hypothyroxinemia. Subclinical hypothyroidism was described as having elevated TSH levels (>4 mIU/L) with normal fT4 concentration (between 10th and 90th percentile in controls), whereas isolated hypothyroxinemia was defined as having normal TSH levels (<=4 mIU/L) along with low fT4 levels (<10th percentile in controls). Subjects with other levels of TSH and fT4 were classified as undefined types of thyroid function, which were excluded from further analysis. In terms of thyroid autoimmunity status, subjects were considered antibody-positive if their anti-TPO levels exceeded 35 IU/mL or their anti-TG levels surpassed 40 IU/mL. Subsequently, we calculated the total number of subjects who remained euthyroid throughout pregnancy, those who experienced intermittent GHT at any visit or persistent GHT across all visits, and those who experienced intermittent thyroid autoimmune positive at any visit or persistent thyroid autoimmune positive across all visits, as defined above.
Covariates

At enrollment, research coordinators interviewed participants to gather information on maternal demographics, pregnancy history, and lifestyle behaviors. In addition, they obtained clinical examination results including blood pressure and anthropometric indices from medical records. Data on infant sex were collected from medical charts, and GA at delivery was determined using ultrasound-verified last menstrual period and date of delivery. Despite matching maternal age and self-identified race/ethnicity between cases and controls, we included maternal age and self-identified race/ethnicity as control variables to ensure conservative estimates.
Statistical analysis

Because subjects with GDM were over-represented in the analytic sample with biomarkers, the sample was reweighted to represent the full cohort (for example, in the reweighted sample 4% of subjects had GDM as opposed to 33% in the nonweighted sample). Weights were measured following the idea of pseudolikelihood in Samuelsen, and aligned with our prior publications.

Crude and weighted characteristics of subjects were calculated in the primary cohort and the nested case-control cohort. All PUFAs were standardized, and both the standardized PUFAs and the raw values of thyroid function biomarkers were analyzed as continuous variables. It is worth mentioning that, as a preliminary step, we calculated the linearity of the assumption regarding involved generating scatterplots of residuals against the fitted values to identify any nonlinear patterns. Once the linearity assumption was verified for all associations investigated, we proceeded with the subsequent statistical analyses as follows: First, we examined the association between early pregnancy PUFAs and thyroid function biomarkers at each visit, using a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) to account for matched case-control pairs. Second, we investigated the visit-specific correlations between early pregnancy PUFAs and thyroid function biomarkers throughout the 4 research visits. This analysis involved incorporating an interaction term with GA in a GLMM, which treated measurements from paired individuals as longitudinal samples in a short term around each research visit and accounted for the random intercept and random slope introduced by pairs. Furthermore, we estimated the relative risk (RR) of experiencing GHT intermittently at any or persistently at all 4 research visits based on the increase in individual standardized plasma phospholipid PUFA levels, using modified Poisson regression. Finally, all regressions mentioned above were performed after applying weights, in both a crude model and a fully adjusted model based on covariates a priori selected covariates: maternal age (years), self-identified race/ethnicity (that is, non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Pacific Islander), maternal education (college degree compared with below college degree), prepregnancy BMI (kg/m2), and maternal smoking (nonsmoker compared with ever or current smoker).

In the sensitivity analysis, we included maternal random glucose level at visit 0, total cholesterol level at visit 0, maternal parity, infant sex, subgroup of SFAs, subgroup of MUFAs, hypertensive disorders during pregnancy (HDP), and GDM as additional covariates. Furthermore, we explored the potential effect modification by maternal prepregnancy BMI. To separate the mechanisms of GHT from autoimmune positive, we further reran the regression by excluding persistent autoimmune positive cases across 4 visits from all participants in the modified Poisson regression. Even though primary analyses were based on hypotheses, not random testing, we still applied false discovery rate (FDR) correction to account for multiple testing. All analyses were performed using R software (version 4.2.1, R Studio, Inc.). The effect sizes were reported as estimates (beta) or RR with a 95% confidence interval (CI) or P value. We defined significance as a 2-tailed P value of 0.05.

Subjects with GDM had a significantly higher prepregnancy BMI, lower prevalence of college education, higher prevalence of family history of diabetes, and shorter GA at delivery, compared with their non-GDM counterparts (Table 1). Given the over-representation of GDM within our subset, we used a reweighting method to accurately represent the original recruited population (Supplemental Table 2).
Early pregnancy plasma phospholipid PUFAs and thyroid function biomarkers in pregnancy

In both crude and fully adjusted models, we observed consistently inverse associations of early pregnancy EPA, n-3 DPA, AA, DTA, and n-6 DPA with the ratio of fT3/fT4, and consistently positive associations of early pregnancy LA, GLA, and DGLA with a ratio of fT3/fT4 across 4 separate research visits during pregnancy (albeit the associations were not always significant) (Supplemental Tables 3 and 4).

FIGURE 2

Supplemental Table 6 presents the multivariable regression analysis of plasma phospholipid PUFAs and the diagnosis of GHT in each research visit, whereas Table 3 and Figure 2 display the regressions of plasma phospholipid PUFAs and GHT across all 4 research visits during pregnancy. Among the significant findings, 3 PUFAs were linked to reduced risks of GHT, whereas 2 PUFAs were associated with increased risks of GHT, respectively. For instance, per SD increment in EPA (SD 0.15%), n-3 DPA (SD 0.20%), and DTA (SD 0.20%) were associated with reduced risks of intermittent GHT (EPA: RR 0.47; 95% CI: 0.32, 0.70; n-3 DPA: 0.71; 0.53, 0.96; and DTA: 0.59; 0.44, 0.79) and persistent GHT (EPA: 0.13; 0.06, 0.28; n-3 DPA: 0.27; 0.14, 0.53; and DTA: 0.24; 0.13, 0.44), respectively (Figure 2, Table 3). Interestingly, per SD increment in n-6 DPA (0.21%) was merely associated with a decreased risk of persistent GHT (0.27; 0.11, 0.65) but not related to intermittent GHT (Figure 2, Table 3). Conversely, per SD increment in EDA (SD 0.10%) was associated with higher risks of persistent GHT alone (2.26; 1.42, 7.50), whereas per SD increment in LA (SD 2.74%) was associated with a higher risk of intermittent GHT alone (1.50; 1.09, 2.07) (Figure 2, Table 3). After FDR correction, most significant associations remained robust except for the inverse association between n-3 DPA and intermittent GHT (Table 3).

To separate the mechanisms of GHT attributed to autoimmune positivity, we performed an additional regression analysis by excluding cases with persistent autoimmune positivity, resulting in 57 and 10 cases of GHT identified at any visit and all visits, respectively. The findings demonstrated comparable effect sizes, as indicated in Supplemental Table 7.

Sensitivity analyses, which involved additional adjustment for maternal plasma random glucose level at visit 0, total cholesterol level at visit 0, maternal parity, infant sex, the sum of SFAs, the sum of MUFAs, HDP, and GDM in the GLMM with repeated measurements did not attenuate any of the significant associations previously identified (Supplemental Tables 8 and 9). Considering the biological correlation between TSH and fT4, we further adjusted for fT4 in all associations with TSH as the outcome, and vice versa. The associations demonstrated similar estimates (Supplemental Table 10). Lastly, we did not observe any effect modification by maternal prepregnancy BMI (Supplemental Table 11).
Discussion

In this prospective study, we identified positive associations of plasma phospholipid EPA and DHA with fT4, along with negative associations with fT3 and ratio of fT3/fT4 throughout pregnancy. In addition, higher levels of plasma phospholipid EPA, DTA, and n-6 DPA were associated with lower risk, whereas LA and EDA were associated with higher risk of GHT. All associations remained statistically significant after multiple testing corrections and sensitivity analyses. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the association between PUFA and thyroid function in pregnancy, as well as the first to assess this relationship with circulating PUFAs in any population, irrespective of pregnancy status.

Thyroid hormones play a pivotal role in both the normal development and function of the thyroid gland and the regulation of metabolism. Should the compensatory mechanism falter, owing to pre-existing maternal conditions or environmental risks, it may lead to impaired thyroid dysfunction, which could manifest in GHT, affecting ~2%-3% of pregnancies. Emerging evidence suggests that dietary choices could potentially influence thyroid function, specifically PUFA-enriched Mediterranean diet.
n-3 PUFAs and gestational thyroid function

Our findings indicated that the majority of n-3 PUFAs had a beneficial association with thyroid function regulation. Specifically, increased levels of EPA and DHA were associated with optimal thyroid function biomarkers, namely lower levels of fT3 and higher levels of fT4. Furthermore, elevated levels of EPA were additionally associated with a lower risk of GHT. Although there is a scarcity of studies investigating the impact of n-3 PUFAs on thyroid function, a recent study showed that a diet rich in n-3 PUFAs may hold potential benefits for individuals with hypothyroidism. In this study, the researchers conducted a cohort of individuals with obesity who followed a diet high in n-3 PUFA and reported a significant increase in fT4 levels after 4 wk of dietary intervention.

The mechanism underlying the elevation of fT4 levels and the reduced risk of GHT could be attributed to the decreased inflammation in vivo induced by higher levels of EPA, n-3 DPA, and DHA. In particular, EPA serves as a substrate for cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase (LO) enzymes, enabling the production of alternative eicosanoids derived from n-3 PUFAs. Although EPA-derived eicosanoids share a similar structure and stability to AA-derived eicosanoids, they are inactive metabolites and exhibit lower proinflammatory activity. Furthermore, apart from their role in producing EPA-derived eicosanoids, n-3 PUFAs also contribute to an anti-inflammatory response, particularly by facilitating the resolution of inflammation. They serve as precursors for a range of lipid mediators, including resolvins, protectins, and maresins, collectively known as "specialized proresolving mediators (SPMs)". These SPMs are synthesized by polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMN) and macrophages during the resolution phase of inflammation. They stimulate important cellular processes such as the cessation of PMN infiltration, the transition of macrophages into an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, and the clearance of apoptotic cells.

Despite the existing evidence suggesting the beneficial regulation of cell functions by PUFAs, the specific biological mechanism linking EPA/DHA to free T3 remains unclear. In some cases of GHT, an increased fT3/fT4 ratio may indicate disruptions in the conversion of T4-T3, associated with thyroid dysfunction. Animal studies have indicated that EPA and AA can undergo metabolism via COX, LO, or epoxygenase pathways, potentially playing a role in preventing i-methyl-2-imidazolethiol-induced hypothyroidism. Contrary to our observation of elevated early pregnancy EPA linked to lower free T3, a previous study in obese subjects showed no significant change in free T3 after n-3 PUFA supplementation, administered twice daily for 4 wk. Future studies are needed to validate our findings and explore the underlying physiology between EPA and free T3.
n-6 PUFAs and gestational thyroid function

In contrast to the production of anti-inflammatory lipid mediators by n-3 PUFAs, the effects of n-6 PUFAs on inflammation are diverse, with the majority contributing to inflammatory processes. Excessive intakes of n-6 PUFAs have been shown to promote the development of various diseases, including inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. Moreover, n-6 PUFAs have been implicated in the initiation of acute inflammation. Consistent with the existing knowledge, our study revealed that AA was associated with reduced levels of fT3, whereas LA and EDA were related to the occurrence of GHT, either intermittently or persistently, throughout pregnancy. The detrimental effects of these n-6 PUFAs on thyroid function may be attributed to various inflammatory pathways, which are hypothesized as follows.

LA is an essential FA through the diet, constituting ~84%-89% of the total dietary intake of PUFAs in the Western diet. One animal study conducted in rats has demonstrated that diets rich in LA, regardless of whether in the trans- or cis-form, led to upregulated expression of lipogenic genes, increased fat mass, and greater adipocyte size and adipocyte number. Interestingly, AA has been suggested as critical for membrane phospholipids in the lymphoid system, and yet, excessive intake of these proinflammatory and prothrombotic n-6 PUFAs has been associated with an increased risk of metabolic diseases. Furthermore, AA also serves as an endogenous ligand that activates peroxisome-proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), which mitigate or inhibit the production of vascular damage, inflammation, lipotoxicity, and endothelial dysfunction. As for EDA, it has been suggested to undergo enzymatic conversion into various eicosanoids, including prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes, lipid mediators involved in inflammation. In addition, EDA may modulate inflammatory signaling pathways such as the nuclear factor-kappa beta signaling pathway, crucial in regulating numerous proinflammatory genes, potentially contributing to increased inflammation levels.

On the contrary, our study also found that 2 specific n-6 PUFAs, DTA, and n-6 DPA, exhibited protective effects against persistent gestational hyperthyroidism throughout pregnancy. Although the specific anti-inflammatory effects and mechanisms of DTA and n-6 DPA are not as extensively studied as n-3 PUFAs such as EPA or DHA, emerging evidence suggests potential anti-inflammatory properties. First, DTA and n-6 DPA can compete with AA for enzymes involved in eicosanoid production. Second, both n-6 PUFAs could modulate inflammatory mediators by inhibiting the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and they may even downregulate the expression and activity of an enzyme involved in the synthesis of inflammatory lipids. However, a comprehensive understanding of the anti-inflammatory properties of DTA and n-6 DPA, particularly their impacts on inflammation-induced GHT, is still required.
Clinical significance

Even though emerging data suggest a beneficial effect of the Mediterranean diet on optimal thyroid function in the general population, evidence relating to circulating n-3 and n-6 PUFAs and thyroid function has been scarce, let alone maternal thyroid function during pregnancy. Our study investigated the relationship between plasma phospholipid n-3 and n-6 PUFAs in early pregnancy and maternal thyroid function biomarkers, as well as the diagnosis of GHT throughout pregnancy, using a longitudinal approach. This unique approach allowed us to identify the associations of different plasma phospholipid PUFAs in relation to maternal thyroid function during pregnancy. Our findings shed light on the distinct roles of plasma phospholipid PUFAs in regulating maternal thyroid function. More importantly, because certain key PUFAs such as EPA, DHA, and AA can be modified through dietary interventions, our data provide valuable evidence suggesting that targeting plasma phospholipid PUFAs may be a potential strategy for intervention to prevent GHT in early pregnancy.
Strength and limitations

Our study has a few notable strengths. The prospective and longitudinal design enabled us to examine the temporal relationships of plasma phospholipid PUFAs in early pregnancy with thyroid function biomarkers and gestational hyperthyroidism throughout the entire gestational period. By including a comprehensive panel of plasma phospholipid PUFAs, we aimed to elucidate the alleged roles of PUFAs in the underlying physiology of maternal thyroid function. By recruiting pregnant subjects from multiple states across the United States, our results could represent better generalizability. However, our study was not without limitations. To begin with, the relatively small sample size of 214 subjects may limit the statistical power of identifying more PUFAs with maternal thyroid function throughout pregnancy. Second, as an observational study, there remains the possibility of residual confounding despite our efforts to control for major known confounders in our analyses. Third, it is worth noting that dietary patterns during pregnancy could potentially modify the associations observed in our study. However, it is important to recognize that factors collected through dietary questionnaires may be susceptible to measurement errors stemming from the subjective nature of selfreporting. Thus, given this concern, the plasma levels of PUFAs, which serve as the main exposures in our study, could effectively represent both exogenous and endogenous sources. Fourth, assessment of thyroid function biomarkers from fasting plasma samples exclusively at visit 1, as opposed to random plasma samples in other research visits (visits 0, 2, and 4). This potential source of variability may bias the trajectory of maternal thyroid function biomarkers. However, in standard clinical or laboratory practice, fasting status is not taken into consideration when measuring thyroid function biomarkers. Last but not least, it is essential to acknowledge that the studied sample may still harbor inherent selection bias, despite the efforts to reweight the sample in the study to mirror the characteristics of the original cohort. Our findings from the present study warrant future studies to confirm the validity.
Conclusion

In summary, our findings revealed distinct associations of individual circulating PUFAs with thyroid regulation during gestation. As certain key PUFAs such as , , and DTA can be modified through dietary interventions, our data offer unique evidence supporting the potential of targeting plasma phospholipid PUFAs for prevention of GHT during early pregnancy.

passages.text: Tyro3 promotes the maturation of glutamatergic synapses

The receptor tyrosine kinase Tyro3 is abundantly expressed in neurons of the neocortex, hippocampus, and striatum, but its role in these cells is unknown. We found that neuronal expression of this receptor was markedly up-regulated in the postnatal mouse neocortex immediately prior to the final development of glutamatergic synapses. In the absence of Tyro3, cortical and hippocampal synapses never completed end-stage differentiation and remained electrophysiologically and ultrastructurally immature. Tyro3-/- cortical neurons also exhibited diminished plasma membrane expression of the GluA2 subunits of AMPA-type glutamate receptors, which are essential to mature synaptic function. Correspondingly, GluA2 membrane insertion in wild-type neurons was stimulated by Gas6, a Tyro3 ligand widely expressed in the postnatal brain. Behaviorally, Tyro3-/- mice displayed learning enhancements in spatial recognition and fear-conditioning assays. Together, these results demonstrate that Tyro3 promotes the functional maturation of glutamatergic synapses by driving plasma membrane translocation of GluA2 AMPA receptor subunits.
Introduction

The three members of the TAM family of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) - Tyro3, Axl, and Mer - were discovered in the early 1990s. Since that time, a great deal has been learned about the important biological functions of the latter two receptors, which are prominently expressed in macrophages, dendritic cells, and other sentinel cells of the immune system. In these cells, Axl and Mer are critical mediators of the phagocytic engulfment and turnover of apoptotic cells and concomitantly, of the intrinsic feedback inhibition of Toll-like receptor and cytokine receptor signaling at the end of the innate immune response. Tyro3 is only modestly expressed by most immune sentinels, but is instead prominently expressed by maturing and mature neurons in the central nervous system (CNS). The roles that Tyro3 might play in these cells, which do not express Axl or Mer, have proven difficult to decipher.

As a family, the TAM receptors exhibit unusual signaling properties relative to other RTKs. Their tyrosine kinase enzymatic activities are stimulated by the binding of two closely-related soluble ligands - Gas6 and Protein S (Pros1) - to the receptor ectodomains. Gas6 activates all three receptors, whereas Pros1 activates Tyro3 and Mer but not Axl. Pros1 also has important activity as an anticoagulant in the blood coagulation cascade, but Gas6 only signals through the three TAM receptors. In addition to ligand binding, full TAM activation also requires the Ca2+-dependent binding of phosphatidylserine (PtdSer), a universal membrane phospholipid, to the amino-terminal 'Gla' domains of the ligands. For example, a Gla-less truncation variant of Gas6 binds Axl with the same sub-nanomolar KD as full-length Gas6, but is entirely incapable of activating the Axl tyrosine kinase. In this respect, TAM receptors and their ligands together act as detectors for PtdSer. This phospholipid is normally sequestered to the cytoplasmic leaflet of plasma membrane bilayers by the action of 'flippases', but is translocated to the extracellular leaflet through the activity of two large families of PtdSer 'scramblases'. These scramblases are activated by caspase cleavage during apoptosis or alternatively, by calcium binding when cells are depolarized. How these special features of Tyro3 signaling might impact its activities in neurons is also unknown.

We have used cell biological and electrophysiological analyses of cortical and hippocampal neurons from wild-type (WT) versus Tyro3-deficient (Tyro3-/-) mice to investigate Tyro3 activities in these cells. We found that in the absence of Tyro3, glutamatergic synapses were both physiologically and ultrastructurally immature. Correspondingly, we observed that Gas6 activation of post-synaptic Tyro3 in WT neurons stimulated the essential plasma membrane insertion of GluA2 AMPA receptor subunits at synapses. We further found that this stimulation was dependent on plasma membrane externalization of PtdSer, which is induced by pre-synaptic depolarization, as Gla-less Gas6 was without effect. Finally, Tyro3-/- mice exhibited behavioral and learning enhancements that are consistent with unusual synaptic plasticity. Together, these observations identify Tyro3 as a mediator of post-synaptic maturation events that are triggered by the pre-synaptic display of phosphatidylserine.
Materials and methods
Mice

C57BL/6 wild-type mice were obtained from The Jackson laboratory. The Tyro3-/- strain has been described previously. All animal procedures were conducted in compliance with the ethical guidelines and according to protocols approved by the Salk Institute Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) (Protocol Nos. 15-0001, 15-0079, and 17-0046).
Hippocampal and cortical neuron culture

Hippocampal and cortical neurons were prepared according to previously described methods, with several modifications. Briefly, hippocampi or cortices from embryonic day 18 (E18) fetuses from timed-pregnant C57BL/6 mice were micro-dissected and chopped into small pieces in Hank's Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS) without Ca2+/Mg2+, with 10 mM HEPES, and then treated with a digestion solution containing HBSS with Ca2+/Mg2+, 10 mM HEPES, 20 units/ml papain and 0.005% DNase for 30 min at 37 C. After digestion, tissues were mechanically dissociated using a pasteur pipette (with tip fire-polished) in HBSS with Ca2+/Mg2+, 10 mM HEPES and trypsin inhibitor. Cell suspensions were plated at 15,000 cells/well on poly-L-lysine precoated glass coverslips (Neuvitro) in 24-well plates for immunocytochemistry, at 150,000/well on poly-L-lysine precoated glass coverslips (Neuvitro) in 24-well plates for electrophysiological recording, and at 106/dish in PLL-coated 35 mm dishes for biochemistry. The cells were maintained in plating media containing Neurobasal  Plus Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 2% B-27  plus supplement (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1% GlutaMAX  supplement (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 5% heat inactivated FBS for 3 h. After attachment of the cells, the media was switched to culturing media, comprised of Neurobasal  Plus Medium, 2% B-27  plus supplement and 1% GlutaMAX  supplement. From 4 days-in-vitro (DIV) onwards, half medium changes were performed with Culturing medium. To inhibit proliferation of glial cells, 0.5 muM cytosine arabinoside (AraC, Sigma-Aldrich) was added to the medium at 4 DIV. Cultures were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 C and 10% CO2.
Hippocampal slice electrophysiology

Acute coronal vibratome slices (350 mum) of postnatal day (P)30-P50 (for field recordings) and P14-16 (for whole cell recordings) C57Bl/6 J mouse hippocampi were prepared and analyzed using standard protocols, as described previously. Briefly, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation and decapitated, and slices were cut into ice-cold cutting solution (in mM: 85 NaCl, 75 sucrose, 2.5 KCl, 0.5 CaCl2, 4 MgCl2, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 25 NaHCO3, 25 glucose, and 2.25 ascorbate) equilibrated with 95% O2/5% CO2. Slices were incubated 30 min at 30 C in oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) (in mM: for whole-cell recording experiments, 126 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 2 MgCl2, 2 CaCl2, 26 NaHCO3, and 18 glucose; for field recording experiments, 126 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 1.3MgSO4, 2.5CaCl2, 26 NaHCO3, and 10 glucose) and maintained at room temperature at least 1 h before being transferred to a submerged recording chamber.

Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) from CA1 pyramidal neurons were conducted at room temperature. Picrotoxin (50 muM) was added to the ACSF to block GABAA receptor-mediated inhibition, and connections between CA3 and CA1 were cut to reduce epileptiform activity. Patch electrodes (3-5 MOmega) were filled with intrapipette solution [in mM: 108 cesium gluconate, 20 Hepes, 0.4 EGTA, 2.8 NaCl, 5 TEACl, 4 MgATP, 0.3 NaGTP, 10 phosphocreatine, adjusted to pH 7.2 with CsOH (290 mosM)]. CA1 pyramidal cells were voltage-clamped at -70 mV, and spontaneous EPSCs (sEPSCs) were recorded. To record mini EPSCs (mEPSCs), 0.5 muM TTX was added to the ACSF.

Field recordings from populations of CA1 neurons were conducted at room temperature using standard methods. Picrotoxin (100 muM) was added to the ACSF to block GABAA receptor-mediated inhibition and connections between CA3 and CA1 were cut to reduce epileptiform activity. Stainless-steel bipolar electrodes were used to stimulate Schaffer collateral fibers (0.05 Hz), and field excitatory postsynaptic potentials (fEPSPs) were recorded from stratum radiatum using extracellular glass microelectrodes (3-5 MOmega) filled with ACSF. Input-output (I/O) relationships were determined by measuring fEPSP (output) amplitudes in relation to stimulation intensity (input). After establishing a stable 20 min baseline, LTP was induced using a high frequency stimulation (HFS) protocol (100 Hz, 1 s duration at test strength). Data are represented normalized to the average fEPSP amplitude 10 min before HFS.
Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from hippocampal neuronal cultures

Cultured hippocampal neurons (13-14 DIV) were prepared as described above. Neurons on glass coverslips were transferred to a recording chamber in standard artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) containing 10 mM HEPES, 4 mM KCl, 2 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgCl2, 139 mM NaCl, 10 mM d-glucose (osmolarity adjusted with sucrose to 320 mOsm, and pH adjusted to 7.4). Cells were patch-clamped with pipettes containing 130 mM K-gluconate, 6 mM KCl, 4 mM NaCl, 10 mM Na-HEPES, 0.2 mM K-EGTA, 0.3 mM GTP, 2 mM Mg-ATP, 0.2 mM cAMP, 10 mM D-glucose, 0.15% biocytin and 0.06% rhodamine, pH 7.2 (pipette tip resistance was 5-8 MOmega). Action potentials were evoked by injecting depolarizing current pulses in current-clamp mode. Spontaneous EPSCs were recorded in voltage-clamp at -60 mV with a 20 kHz sampling rate with inhibitory activity blocked by 40 muM bicuculline. Signals were amplified with a Multiclamp700B amplifier and recorded with Clampex 10.4 software (Axon Instruments). Miniature EPSCs were recorded also in voltage-clamp mode but with the addition of 0.5 muM TTX. Data were subjected to a 3,000 Hz low-pass filter and analyzed using Clampfit-10 and the software package Matlab (2014A, The MathWorks Inc., Natick, MA, 2000). All measurements were conducted at room temperature.
Cortical neuron treatments

Primary cortical neurons were cultured for 11 DIV before starting treatment with either 20 nM Gas6 or 20 nM Gla-less Gas6. For 7 day long-term treatment, cortical neurons were treated starting at 11 DIV with supplement every other day when medium was half changed. For 1 day-short term treatment, 20 nM Gas6 were added only once to cultures at 16 DIV with or without pretreatment using 100 nM Purified Recombinant Annexin V (BD Pharmingen, #556416). Treatment with TBS buffer, the solvent for Gas6, were used as negative control. To visualize exposed phosphatidylserine on plasma membrane during neuron development in vitro, cortical neurons at 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, or 20 days in vitro (DIV) were incubated with pSIVA-IANBD (Novus Biologicals, NBP2-29382) diluted to 20 mul/ml and CellTracker Red CMTPX dye (Invitrogen C34552) at 0.5 muM in culture medium for 60 min at 37 C, 10% CO2 before fixing with 4%PFA. To stain exposed phosphatidylserine after calcium ionophore A23187 treatment, cortical neurons at 18 DIV were treated with A23187 at concentration of 5 muM for 20 min in medium also containing pSIVA-IANBD diluted to 20 mul/ml and 0.5 mM CellTracker Red CMTPX dye before fixing with 4% PFA.
GluA2 live staining in mouse cortical neurons

Mouse cortical neurons were live stained for GluA2 according to previously described methods, with several modifications. Briefly, cortical neurons on coverslips were incubated with mouse anti-GluA2 (Millipore MAB397) at a 1:100 dilution and CellTracker Red CMTPX dye (Invitrogen C34552) at a 0.5 mM concentration in culture medium for 30 min at 37 C, 10% CO2. After washing with DPBS and fixing with pre-warmed (34 C) 4% PFA for 5 min, the coverslips were washed with PBS and then blocked (without permeabilizing) with PBS containing 2% BSA and 5% normal goat serum for 1 h at room temperature in a humidified chamber. After blocking, coverslips were incubated with goat anti-mouse Alexa 488 at 1:500 dilution in PBS containing 2% BSA and 5% normal goat serum for 3 h at room temperature. Coverslips were then washed with PBS and mounted in Prolong Diamond antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Molecular Probe REF P36962). Neurons were imaged on Zeiss LSM700 using the 63x oil-immersion objective. At least 45 cells per condition were imaged across three coverslips in each independent experiment. A minimum of 3 independent experiments were run. Cells were located using CellTracker Red CMTPX in the red channel. Exposure acquisition was set according to neurons with Gas6 treatment within each independent experiment, capturing 16 bit images at a resolution of 1024x1024 pixels. GluA2 puncta on the soma and dendrites of cortical neurons were analyzed using Imaris software and normalized to cell volume that was calculated based on CellTracker Red signals.
Perfusion and tissue processing for electron microscopy

Mice were anesthetized with 2.5% Avertin/Saline IP, and then dissected open from the abdomen up into the chest cavity. The right atrium was nicked and perfusion was performed through the left ventricle with the following solutions: 1 x 1' Ringers at 37 C, 1 x 9' 2.5% glut/2.0% Para/1 mM CaCl2/ 0.15 M Caco. pH7.3 at 37 C. The brain was cut with a razor blade in a coronal plain using the "brain jig." Cuts were made at 4 mm anterior and 5 mm posterior in the brain jig. First fixing was performed for 2 h at 4 C in 2.5% glut/2.0% Para/1 mM CaCl2/0.15 M Caco. pH7.3. The brain was embedded in 2.5% agar/0.15 M Caco then mounted with super glue on a stub for cutting. Coronal sections (300 mum) were cut through the brain in pairs. Sections were placed in a 12 well plate with 0.15 M caco buffer pH 7.3. Sections were washed overnight in 0.15 M caco buffer pH 7.3 at 4 C, and slices were trimmed down to the specific hippocampus area of interest in the CA1 region just above dentate gyrus. In a second fixing, the trimmed sections were incubated in 2% Osmium Tetroxide/0.15 M caco. pH7.3 for 3 h on ice in a fume hood, followed by 5 times washing in milli-Q water on ice. A third fixation was performed in 2% Uranyl Acetate for 45 min on ice. Dehydration was performed in 30, 50, 70, 95% ETOH (in sequence) for 8 min each and in 100% ETOH twice for 8 min each, and then in acetonitrile. Infiltration was performed in 66/33 ratio of resin/acetonitrile for 30 min, in Epon/Araldite for 2 h at room temperature (RT), and then in Epon/Araldite for 3 h at RT. Embedding was performed in fresh resin using flat embedding capsules at 65 C overnight.
Electron microscopy image analyses

Synapses were defined by the presence of a stained postsynaptic density facing (apposed to) a presynaptic process containing at least three synaptic vesicles. Perforated synapses were defined by the presence of a discontinuity in the postsynaptic density, and multiple synapse boutons (MSBs) were defined by the presence of at least 2 independent dendritic spines contacting the same axon terminal. Three sections were analyzed per block, and 2 blocks per animal were used to collect micrographs. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) micrographs were taken on a Zeiss Libra 120 microscope operated at 80 kV, using a Gatan Ultrascan 4,000 camera at 4 K resolution at an initial magnification of 4,000x, and enlarged photographically to a final magnification of 21,700x. Synapses were randomly photographed in an area corresponding to the stratum radiatum (boxed in Figure 1D), the suprapyramidal region of the hippocampus that contains CA3-to-CA1 Schaffer collaterals. The density of perforated synapses and MSBs were estimated by two independent observers who were blind to genotype.

Volumetric data from serial sections in the scanning electron microscope (SEM; S3EM) were also collected. Briefly, resin embedded samples from control and Tyro3-/- conditions were selected, the stratum radiatum was identified from semi-thin sections, and a frustum of 150 x 400 x 60 mum was trimmed using a Leica UC7 ultramicrotome. A silicon chip (35 x 7 mm, University Wafer, Boston, MA) was glow discharged in a plasma cleaner (Harrick, Ithaca), rinsed in deionized water, and partially immersed in a Diatome Histo knife. An ionizing gun (Leica EM Crion) was activated and oriented toward the cutting edge of the knife mounted on the ultramicrotome. Ribbons of approximately 100 serial sections of 50 nm thickness were cut, the water level was slowly lowered, and sections were allowed to dry on the silicon. Samples were mounted using carbon sticky tabs and loaded into a Zeiss Sigma VP SEM, and serial sections were imaged using the array tomography software module of Atlas5 (FIBICS, Ottawa). A region of interest unobstructed by artifact throughout the series was identified and 2 nm/px images were collected on consecutive sections. Images were aligned using rigid and affine alignment functions available in TrakEM2 in Fiji. Evaluation of datasets and segmentation of dendritic spines was conducted in Reconstruct. The serial 2D segments were exported as VRML mesh files and imported into Blender software1 for further visualization.
Subcellular fractionation

Subcellular fractions of P30 hippocampus were obtained using established protocols, as described previously. Briefly, animals were anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation and decapitated, brains were quickly removed, and hippocampi were dissected out and homogenized in 10 vol of Hepes sucrose buffer (0.32 M sucrose and 4 mM Hepes, pH 7.4) supplemented with protease inhibitor mixture (Complete, Roche) using a glass- Teflon homogenizer at 900 rpm (12 strokes). The homogenate was centrifuged for 10 min at 1,000 x g, and the pellet (P1) containing the nuclei was discarded. The supernatant (S1) was centrifuged for 20 min at 10,000 x g, resulting in a crude synaptosomal pellet (P2). P2 was resuspended in 10 vol of Hepes sucrose buffer and centrifuged for 10 min at 20,000 x g, resulting in a washed crude synaptosomal pellet (P2'). P2' was lysed by hypo-osmotic shock in water and adjusted to 4 mM Hepes. After 30 min of gentle rotation at 4 C, P2' was centrifuged for 20 min at 25,000 x g, resulting in a crude synaptosomal membrane fraction (P3) and a crude synaptic vesicle fraction (S3). Aliquots were collected at multiple steps of the fractionation and solubilized in Triton X-100 (1%) for Western blot analysis. PSD-enriched fractions were prepared as described previously.
SDS-PAGE and western blot

Protein samples were prepared with reducing Laemmli buffer and boiled for 10 min at 95 C, and then separated on NuPAGE 4-12% Bis-Tris Mini protein gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific NP0323BOX) for 3 h at constant voltage of 90 V. After gel electrophoresis, proteins were transferred onto Immobilon-P PVDF membranes (Millipore IPVH00010) for 90 min at constant current of 0.4A. Membranes were blocked with 1x Tris Buffered Saline (TBS) with 1% Casein (BioRad, #1610782) for 1 h at room temperature in gentle shaking, and then incubated at 4 C overnight with the primary antibody in blocking buffer, rabbit anti-Tyro3 (Cell signaling 5585S) at a dilution of 1:2000, mouse anti-PSD95 (Thermo Fisher Scientific MA1-046) at a dilution of 1:2000, mouse anti-GluA2 (Millipore MAB397) at a dilution of 1:5000, rabbit anti-synaptophysin (Abcam ab16659), or mouse anti-GAPDH (Santa Cruz SC-32233) at a dilution of 1:10,000. After washing with TBS buffer containing 0.1% Tween-20, membranes were incubated with secondary antibody for 3 h at room temperature (Peroxidase AffiniPure Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG, Jackson Immunoresearch 111-036-047 or 115-006-072). After washing with TBS buffer containing 0.1% Tween-20, membranes were incubated in chemiluminescent substrate (SuperSignal, ThermoFisher 34,580) and the chemiluminescent signal was detected and recorded by exposure of the membrane to X-ray film.
Open field tests

Mice (male, age 3 months) were placed in a novel open field [16'' (W) x 16'' (D) x 15'' (H)] and allowed to explore it for a period of 20 min. Horizontal and vertical movement were automatically tracked utilizing 2 parallel infrared beam arrays surrounding a Plexiglas arena. The total distance the mice traveled, and percentage time they spent in peripheral and center regions of the open filed were analyzed.
Morris water maze

In the hidden version of the Morris water maze test, mice (male, age 3 months) were trained with two blocks per day over 10 days, with each block consisting of two trials with 30 s interval between the trials. The platform was hidden 1 cm below the surface of water made opaque with white nontoxic paint. Starting points were changed every trial and every day. In each trial, mice were given 60 s to find the platform. If mice found the platform earlier than 60 s, the trial ended then. If mice failed to find the platform, the trial terminated at 60s and they were guided to reach the platform. After mice had reached platform, they were allowed to rest on it for 10 s. On the 11th day, the platform was removed for a 60 s probe trial. Swim path length and speed were recorded (Ethovision; Noldus Information Technology, Wageningen, The Netherlands).
Contextual fear conditioning

Prior to behavioral procedures, mice aged at 3 months were acclimatized to the testing room and handled by the experimenter for 1 week. On the eighth day (experimental day 1), mice were allowed to explore the context A for 10 min. On day 2, the mice were placed into context A for fear conditioning for a total time of 42 s. The mice were firstly permitted 10s to explore the context, and then presented with 2 s 0.7 mA electric shocks to the foot followed by 30s rest before return to home cage. On day 3, freezing behaviors were monitored first in conditioned context A for 5 min, and 90 min later in a novel context B for another 5 min.
Quantification and statistical analysis

Results are expressed as mean +- s.e.m. Statistical analysis was carried out in Prism 9.1.0 (Graph-Pad, La Jolla, CA, USA). A two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test was used for statistical comparisons between two groups. For analysis of Morris water maze and contextual fear conditioning tests, a two-way repeated measures ANOVA was used. Bonferroni's multiple comparisons test was used for post hoc analyses. Sample sizes were chosen based on previous studies. No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes.
Results
Neuronal Tyro3 expression in the postnatal brain

We first confirmed several unusual features of Tyro3 expression that have been reported previously. As for the other members of the TAM family, multiple studies have documented only limited expression of Tyro3 in developing mouse and rat embryos. Instead, a substantial up-regulation in the expression of this RTK, which is largely restricted to neurons in the neocortex, hippocampus, and other higher centers of the brain, was detected by western blot in the mouse cortex during the first 2 weeks of postnatal life (Figure 1A). High Tyro3 expression was maintained in the adult brain (Figure 1A). With respect to the results presented below, it is important to note that this time course of cortical up-regulation immediately precedes the time course of the maturation of glutamatergic synapses, as monitored by expression of the post-synaptic scaffolding protein PSD-95, the synaptic vesicle protein synaptophysin, and the GluA2 subunit of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Figure 1A). The maturation of glutamatergic synapses has previously been shown to be dependent upon the de novo plasma membrane insertion of these calcium-impermeable GluA2 subunits, and in the mouse, this occurs between postnatal day (P)7 and P16. Although Tyro3 mRNA has been detected in select immune and tumor cells, and in newborn oligodendrocytes, it is overwhelmingly the product of adult neurons in the brain (; Figures 1B,C). While Tyro3 mRNA is abundant in neurons across all layers of the adult neocortex (Figures 1B,C), and in striatum (Figure 1C) and hippocampus (Figures 1B,D), it is not significantly expressed in the thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, or spinal cord.

Neuronal expression of Tyro3 has previously been shown to exhibit a marked disparity across the fields of the adult hippocampus, with very high expression in CA1, very low expression in CA3, and no expression in CA2 (Figure 1D). [Tyro3 was among the first identified molecular markers that distinguish CA1 neurons in the hippocampus ]. Staining of adult mouse hippocampal sections with a Tyro3 antibody revealed that Tyro3 protein was abundant in both the apical and basal processes of CA1 neurons (Figure 1E), as has previously been reported for cortical neurons. When we performed densitometric biochemical fractionation of membranes from P30 mouse hippocampus (see Methods), we observed that Tyro3 largely, although not exclusively, co-fractionated with post-synaptic rather than pre-synaptic markers (Figure 1F), consistent with its previously observed localization to neuronal dendrites in the neocortex. This localization is also consistent with the Tyro3 activation of post-synaptic protein kinase C and other kinases that has been observed in a mouse model of frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

As noted above, the Tyro3 tyrosine kinase is activated by two closely-related, secreted (soluble) extracellular ligands - Gas6 and Protein S (Pros1) - both of whose mRNAs are very widely expressed across many different cell types in the CNS. In addition to their expression in neurons, the Gas6 and Pros1 mRNAs are abundant in all microglia, where they regulate multiple microglial properties, and in brain endothelial cells 2.

As also noted above, the final component that is essential for TAM receptor activation and signaling is the membrane glycerophospholipid phosphatidylserine (PtdSer). The N-terminal 'Gla' domains of Gas6 and Pros1 bind to PtdSer, whereas the C-terminal 'SHBG' domains of these ligands bind to the Ig domains of the TAM receptor ectodomains. In plasma membranes, a set of flippase enzymes normally confines PtdSer to the inner leaflet of the membrane bilayer, but in neurons and all other cells, PtdSer is translocated to the outer leaflet by the action of both Ca2+- and caspase-activated scramblases. Effective TAM signaling cannot occur in the absence of PtdSer externalization, as it is the only way in which this phospholipid can access the Gla domains of Gas6 and Pros1.

We visualized PtdSer externalization in cultured cortical neurons using pSIVA, a 'polarity-sensitive indicator for viability and apoptosis', derived from Annexin B12, which fluoresces strongly only when bound to PtdSer. Neurons were isolated from embryonic day (E)18 cortices, and cultured in vitro using established protocols. As has been described previously, we found that these cells underwent maturation over the first 14 days in vitro (DIV), marked by the up-regulation of Tyro3, GluA2, and PSD-95 by 11 DIV (Supplementary Figure S1A). This in vitro time course paralleled the expression of these same markers in vivo (Figure 1A). Incubation of differentiating cortical neurons with pSIVA revealed that prominent PtdSer externalization occurred between 16 and 20 DIV (Supplementary Figures S1B,C) - when synaptogenesis and spontaneous electrical activity are robust. This externalized PtdSer was frequently seen to be localized on neuronal membrane overlying puncta of presynaptic synaptophysin (Supplementary Figure S1D). Spontaneous electrical activity allows for calcium influx and the activation of Ca2+-dependent scramblases, which are the enzymes that translocate PtdSer to the membrane surface. These scramblases can also be artificially activated by calcium ionophores. When we strongly activated Ca2+ influx in 18 DIV cortical neurons using the calcium ionophore A23187 (5 muM for 20 min), we triggered massive PtdSer externalization onto the surface of these cells without inducing cell death (Figure 1G).

Together, the above results demonstrate that all of the essential components of TAM signaling - Tyro3, the ligands Gas6 and Pros1, and PtdSer - are mobilized in and around neurons of the maturing postnatal brain. It is important to note that in most settings the tripartite complex of PtdSer-TAM ligand-TAM receptor has been found to link the membranes of two apposed cells, with PtdSer on one cell, a TAM receptor on the apposed cell, and a TAM ligand bridged between. As discussed below, it is likely that such a tripartite PtdSer-Gas6-Tyro3 bridging complex links the apposed pre- and post-synaptic membranes of active synapses.
Immature physiology of Tyro3-/- synapses

We have previously described the generation and analysis of full germline mouse loss-of-function mutants for Tyro3. Tyro3-/- mice are born in Mendelian ratios, have normal life spans, are fertile as males and females, and display superficially normal histology in the brain and other tissues (; but see). They are full-length protein nulls (Figure 1E). Given the localized expression of Tyro3 in neurons of the hippocampus (Figures 1B,D), we first examined the physiology of the synaptic connection between pre-synaptic CA3 neurons and post-synaptic CA1 neurons - the 'Schaffer collaterals' - in standard ex vivo hippocampal slice preparations prepared from male WT versus Tyro3-/- brains (Figure 2A; see Methods). At this synapse, Tyro3 presumably acts post-synaptically, since it is abundantly expressed on the pyramidal dendrites of CA1 neurons, but not by CA3 neurons (Figures 1B,D,E). We stimulated the Schaffer collaterals and recorded field excitatory postsynaptic potentials (fEPSPs), spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs), and miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents [mEPSCs, recorded in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX)] in CA1 (Figure 2A) (see Methods).
